item.title: The Elements of Style
item.description:
• Succinct version of Grammar Rules and Mechanics that we can use in day-to-day life.

Elementary rules of usage

Usage of ’s

  • Form possessive singular of nouns by adding ’s.
    • Exceptions are possessive of ancient proper names ending in -is and -es. e.g. Jesus’, Achilles’, Moses’ etc.
      • e.g. the laws of Moses, the temple of Isis etc.
    • Pronomial possessives have no apostrophe. e.g. hers, its, etc.
      • it’s == it is.
      • its == possessive
    • Indefinite pronouns use the apostrophe to show possession. e.g. one’s rights.

Usage of comma

  • Use paranthetic expressions between commas.

    • A name or a title in direct address is paranthetic.
      • e.g. Well, Susan, this is a fine mess you are in.
    • If interruption to the flow of sentence is slight, commas may be safely omitted.
    • Abbreviations etc., i.e., and e.g., the abbreviations for academic degrees, and titles that follow a name are paranthetic.
      • e.g. Letters, packages, etc., should go here.
      • e.g. Horace Fulsome, Ph.D., presided.
    • Comma shouldn’t separate a noun from restrictive term of identification.
      • e.g. Billy the Kid, The poet Sappho, James Wright Jr etc.
    • Non-restrictive clause, one that doesn’t serve to identify or define the antecedent noun, are parenthetic.
      • Clauses introduced by which, when, and where are nonrestrictive. They don’t limit or define, merely add something.
      • Similar clauses introduced by conjunctions indicating time or place are paranthetic too.
        • e.g. In 1769, when Napoleon was born, …
        • e.g. The audience, which had at first been indifferent, …
      • e.g. Uncle Bert, being slightly deaf, moved forward …
    • Restrictive clauses are not paranthetic.
      • e.g. People who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones.
      • e.g. People sitting in the rear couldn’t hear, …

  • Place a comma before conjunction introducing an independent clause.

    • e.g. The situation is perilous, but there is still one chance of escape.

  • April 6, 1998 but 6 April 1988

item.title: How to read a book
item.description:
Quotes

On ignorance

An abecedarian ignorance that precedes knowledge, and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it.” The first is the ignorance of those who, not knowing their ABC’s, cannot read at all. The second is the ignorance of those who have misread many books. – Montaigne

On readiness and habit

The difference between your activity before and after you have formed a habit is a difference in facility and readiness.
